scope: SCOPED: IPv4 codec version/checksum/TTL validation and transport parameters, bounded option parsing, selected source-route origin/final-destination helpers including old-encoding return-route tolerance, Record Route and Timestamp helpers, and ARP (section 2.3.2): the ntcp-arp cache's validation and per-destination request rate limit (2.3.2.1), and the 2.3.2.2 packet queue of ntcp-native Ethernet ports that resolve IPv4 next hops by ARP, which keep each owner's latest frame while its next hop resolves and send it once resolved (ntcp-socket's IPv4 ports still use static neighbours). RFC6864 amends Identification for atomic datagrams. No full-document or full IPv4 host conformance: forwarding/routing, fragmentation/reassembly (but for the section 3.3.2 reassembly timeout recommendation, recorded as an exception), security facilities, address administration, legacy ToS policy, other ARP embeddings and general host/socket APIs are outside this inventory.

paragraphs.quote: An implementation of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) [LINK:2] MUST provide a mechanism to flush out-of-date cache entries. If this mechanism involves a timeout, it SHOULD be possible to configure the timeout value.
paragraphs.reason: ArpCache ages REACHABLE entries to STALE after a ReachableTime drawn from [0.5, 1.5) times base_reachable, revalidates a used STALE entry through DELAY and unicast PROBE, and deletes it one RetransTimer after the last unanswered probe; incomplete resolutions fail likewise. Every timer is an ArpTimers field in milliseconds, converted to caller units.

paragraphs.quote: A mechanism to prevent ARP flooding (repeatedly sending an ARP Request for the same IP address, at a high rate) MUST be included. The recommended maximum rate is 1 per second per destination.
paragraphs.reason: Only ArpCache::next_control originates requests, and each request to a destination reported possibly or definitely submitted defers that destination's next one by RetransTimer (1 s default); blocked or failed attempts consume nothing. Re-resolving never sends sooner, and a failed destination is retried only one RetransTimer after its last request.

paragraphs.quote: The link layer SHOULD save (rather than discard) at least one (the latest) packet of each set of packets destined to the same unresolved IP address, and transmit the saved packet when the address has been resolved.
paragraphs.reason: On an ntcp-native Ethernet port that resolves IPv4 next hops by ARP, a frame whose next hop Host::resolve_neighbor holds stays in its owner's one transmit slot (the owner's latest output) without a submission ticket; ntcp-arp records one held tag per owner, and Host::neighbor_wake's Retry resends that frame through egress once the reply arrives, while Unreachable withdraws it unsubmitted with the soft Address Unreachable advice. The native test asserts that the first SYN waits while only the broadcast request leaves and is sent to the replying station's MAC once the reply arrives; the kernel-interop test (tests/linux_arp.py) completes TCP with Linux with no static neighbour. ntcp-socket's IPv4 ports still use static neighbours.

paragraphs.quote: A datagram whose version number is not 4 MUST be silently discarded.
paragraphs.reason: The codec returns Version without exposing a decoded packet or generating a response; all non-4 version nibbles are asserted.

paragraphs.quote: A host MUST verify the IP header checksum on every received datagram and silently discard every datagram that has a bad checksum.
paragraphs.reason: Every parse and quoted-header bounds check verifies the full header checksum, including options, before returning metadata; the codec has no response side effect.

paragraphs.quote: A host MUST NOT send a datagram with a Time-to-Live (TTL) value of zero.
paragraphs.reason: Encoder rejects zero TTL without modifying the output buffer.

paragraphs.quote: A host MUST NOT discard a datagram just because it was received with TTL less than 2.
paragraphs.reason: Endpoint parsing accepts every TTL, including zero and one, after structural and checksum validation; originating TTL zero remains invalid.

paragraphs.quote: The IP layer MUST provide a means for the transport layer to set the TTL field of every datagram that is sent. When a fixed TTL value is used, it MUST be configurable. The current suggested value will be published in the "Assigned Numbers" RFC.
paragraphs.reason: Transmit.hop_limit is a per-datagram transport parameter; codec assertions use 1, 64 and 255. This selected codec interface does not claim a complete host configuration API.

paragraphs.quote: There MUST be a means for the transport layer to specify IP options to be included in transmitted IP datagrams (see Section 3.4).
paragraphs.reason: Transmit.ipv4_options configures the supported options, which encode emits in the IPv4 header; full and shared headers agree with full wire lengths.

paragraphs.quote: All IP options (except NOP or END-OF-LIST) received in datagrams MUST be passed to the transport layer (or to ICMP processing when the datagram is an ICMP message). The IP and transport layer MUST each interpret those IP options that they understand and silently ignore the others.
paragraphs.reason: Host::process, the single destination-processing step after reassembly, keeps every validated option except NOP/EOL in the processed envelope that TCP and every ICMP consumer (Echo, errors, Source Quench classification, the Echo adjunct) receive, in every enabled receive profile whatever its RR/TS interpretation or source-route admission; native managed input, its host-less parser and the example hand on the same options. The Host interprets Record Route, Timestamp and source routes, TCP interprets only a source route (its return route), the Echo service continues RR/TS and reverses an authorized route, and every other option is delivered and silently ignored, never reflected. Host, codec, native and example tests and the integration/rfc_host ip-options cases cover whole and reassembled datagrams with known and opaque options.

paragraphs.quote: The IP layer must not crash as the result of an option length that is outside the possible range. For example, erroneous option lengths have been observed to put some IP implementations into infinite loops.
paragraphs.reason: Lengths are bounds checked before advancing or slicing; malformed examples and exhaustive one-byte length/pointer combinations terminate safely.

paragraphs.quote: A host MUST support originating a source route and MUST be able to act as the final destination of a source route.
paragraphs.reason: Selected source-route-enabled codec profile originates strict/loose wire routes and accepts completed routes at the final endpoint. Intermediate-hop forwarding and fragmentation remain outside scope.

paragraphs.quote: If host receives a datagram containing a completed source route (i.e., the pointer points beyond the last field), the datagram has reached its final destination; the option as received (the recorded route) MUST be passed up to the transport layer (or to ICMP message processing). This recorded route will be reversed and used to form a return source route for reply datagrams (see discussion of IP Options in Section 4). When a return source route is built, it MUST be correctly formed even if the recorded route included the source host (see case (B) in the discussion below).
paragraphs.reason: The selected codec returns the completed route unchanged in Packet.ipv4_options. Its return_route helper reverses the recorded hops and removes a legacy first source-host entry; reply header assertions cover both encodings and strict/loose routes.

paragraphs.quote: An IP header containing more than one Source Route option MUST NOT be sent; the effect on routing of multiple Source Route options is implementation-specific.
paragraphs.reason: OutgoingIpv4Options has a single source_route field; all strict/loose output assertions decode exactly one source-route option.

paragraphs.quote: Implementation of originating and processing the Record Route option is OPTIONAL.
paragraphs.reason: This optional capability is selected: tests originate zero slots, then record source/destination addresses with fixed option length and bounded pointers.

paragraphs.quote: Implementation of originating and processing the Timestamp option is OPTIONAL. If it is implemented, the following rules apply:
paragraphs.reason: This optional capability is selected, with its following origin/destination/value rules inventoried separately and gaps retained as TODOs.

paragraphs.quote: The originating host MUST record a timestamp in a Timestamp option whose Internet address fields are not pre-specified or whose first pre-specified address is the host's interface address.
paragraphs.reason: Encoding records the source for flags 0/1 and for a matching first prespecified address; nonmatching prespecified addresses remain unrecorded.

paragraphs.quote: The destination host MUST (if possible) add the current timestamp to a Timestamp option before passing the option to the transport layer or to ICMP for processing.
paragraphs.reason: Where Timestamp processing is implemented (the interpreting profile; the disabled profile declines that OPTIONAL processing and still delivers every option), Host::process records this host's timestamp once per complete datagram after reassembly, before TCP and every ICMP consumer, sampling the embedding's Ipv4TimestampProvider only for a slot this host may write and keeping the slot when no time is available. Native managed input and the example supply the characterized Linux UTC provider's time, standard or high-bit-marked nonstandard elapsed time, so lacking UTC never skips a write; retained, deferred and replayed input is never recorded again. Host, native and example tests and the integration/rfc_host ip-options cases (a peer's Timestamp returned updated by each embedding) cover it; the stateless compatibility parsers (ntcp_ip::parse, the host-less native parser, the full-frame ICMP decoders) make no destination-processing claim.

paragraphs.quote: A timestamp value MUST follow the rules given in Section 3.2.2.8 for the ICMP Timestamp message.
paragraphs.reason: Local writes enforce UTC day range or a nonstandard high bit. The characterized Linux UTC provider (ntcp-clock) emits UTC milliseconds since midnight only when its one read-only adjtimex acquisition shows no kernel error status and neither TIME_ERROR nor TIME_OOP, a maximum error within the kernel's 16 s phase limit (accuracy within a few minutes under RFC1122 section 3.2.2.8, conditional on the time daemon's bound and the kernel drift model being truthful), a consistent BOOTTIME bracket of at most 64 ms (at most the six low-order bits undefined) and no unconfirmed suspend; otherwise it emits high-bit-marked elapsed time. Recorded kernel facts test every state, error predicate, limit, failure, decoding, step, bracket and suspend case; actual samples are checked against their own facts, and a bounded characterization shows sub-1/15-second progression of the returned time, at least 15 updates/second, on the tested system, never inferred from clock_getres or numeric range. Native records arriving datagrams with the provider and originates no IPv4 options; the example records and originates with it, sampling only for a slot it writes; their tests and the integration/rfc_host cases accept an unmarked value only within the evidence's own healthy adjtimex window. Low-level u32 interfaces remain documented caller contracts.

paragraphs.quote: It is recommended that the value lie between 60 seconds and 120 seconds.
paragraphs.reason: Deliberate Linux-compatible deviation: the IPv4 reassembly timeout of ntcp-native Networks is 30 seconds, Linux's ipfrag_time, below this recommended range. It is a fixed value, never set from the remaining TTL, and the Host's ReassemblyLimits::ipv4_timeout_seconds accepts any nonzero value. The fragments of one datagram leave its sender together, so a shorter hold rarely discards a datagram that would have completed; it frees the slots that lost fragments pin sooner and shortens the time in which a reused 16-bit Identification can join fragments of different datagrams. IPv6 keeps the 60 seconds of RFC 8200 section 4.5.

paragraphs.quote: When sending an identical copy of an earlier datagram, a host MAY optionally retain the same Identification field in the copy.
paragraphs.reason: RFC6864 amends Identification semantics. Selected atomic datagrams may use arbitrary IDs, including repeated zero; non-atomic copies, allocation and reassembly are outside this scoped inventory.
